newsitem.title: USA: Procter to buy Tambrands for $1.85 billion.
newsitem.headline: Procter to buy Tambrands for $1.85 billion.

text.p: U.S. Consumer products company Procter & Gamble Co. said on Wednesday it will acquire Tambrands Inc. and its Tampax tampon brand for $1.85 billion, expanding its worldwide marketing of feminine hygiene products.
Procter & Gamble, which makes such personal care products as Pampers disposable diapers, Pantene hair care and Oil of Olay for skin care, said it bid $50 a share for Tambrands.

Tambrands, based in White Plains, N.Y., has manufactured Tampax tampons for more than 60 years and has 44 percent of the tampon market, the companies said in a news release. The company reported 1996 sales of $662 million.
Procter & Gamble said it expects to reap about $100 million in annual savings within three years from the acquisition.

"There is certainly going to be savings in the first year because there are certain redundant administrative costs, selling costs that will be eliminated fairly quickly," Procter & Gamble Vice President Clayton Daley Jr. said in a telephone interview. "Other things will take a little more time to get to."

Other savings will come over time as Procter & Gamble applies its so-called efficient consumer response initiatives to Tambrands and its Tampax tampon. This includes efforts such as continuous product replenishment, just-in-time inventory management and more efficient promotions and assortment.
Analysts said the deal was positive for both companies.
Tambrands shares rose $2 to $48 a share and Procter & Gamble gained $4 to $119.75, both on the New York Stock Exchange.

In a statement, Tambrands Chairman Edward Fogarty said, "Becoming part of P&G -- a world-class company with global marketing and distribution capabilities -- will accelerate the global growth of Tampax and enable the brand to achieve its full potential."

One particular advantage in the deal, analysts said, is that Procter & Gamble could expand marketing of Tampax in emerging nations. About 90 percent of Tampax's business currently is in North America and Europe.
"You might think of the U.S. and Europe as the financial drivers behind the deal short term," Daley said. "Long term the opportunities are in developing markets."
The problem Procter & Gamble may face, however, is the difficulty of promoting Tampax in some cultures where discussing a feminine hygiene product may be a taboo.

"The (cultural) differences are critical. With a feminine hygiene products like tampons, it may be a touchy subject in some markets," said Pradeep Chintagunta, professor of marketing at the University of Chicago, Graduate School of Business.
Daley acknowledged that expanding in emerging markets will require investments in school programmes, product sampling, marketing and consumer education.

"In my view, it is going to take quite a while to re-educate consumers in the emerging markets into using tampons," JP Morgan analyst Michael Grant added. "P&G has the marketing know-how and the money to make that happen."
Daley said his company has reaped success in overseas markets with products like its Whisper feminine pad in Asia and Pantene hair care products.
For established markets, Procter & Gamble will increase development spending behind Tampax, Daley added.
While antitrust clearance for the Tambrands acquisition is not completely assured, the deal is expected to be approved, Daley said. "We are confident from an antitrust standpoint."
Previously, Tambrands stock had been unusually active in the last few days as rumours of a possible acquisition by Procter & Gamble circulated through Wall Street.
Tambrand shares traded at $43.50 a week ago and traders at the Chicago Board Options Exchange said Tuesday trading in Tambrands options was unusually active in the last few days.
